0.title: Trembling Love Before a Holy God
0.overview:
Few phrases in the Bible are repeated as often as this one, and few are less understood today. The fear of the LORD is called the beginning of wisdom (Ps 111:10), a fountain of life (Prov 14:27) and the whole duty of man (Eccl 12:13). Yet many Christians are unsure what it means. Some think it belongs to the Old Testament and was replaced by love in the New. Others quietly assume it means being afraid that God is waiting to punish them. Many simply never think about it.

Scripture's answer is richer than either error. The fear of the Lord is the right response of a creature to the holy, majestic and gracious God. It includes awe at his greatness, reverence for his holiness, a sober awareness that he is the Judge of all, and a deep desire not to grieve him. In the believer it is not the cringing dread of a slave before a cruel master. It is the trembling love of a child before a Father who is also the King of the universe.

The New Testament does not abolish this fear. The early church grew walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit (Acts 9:31). Peter tells believers who call God Father to conduct yourselves with fear throughout the time of your exile (1 Pet 1:17). And the prophet said that the Messiah himself would delight in it: And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD (Isa 11:3).

Why does this matter? Because what we fear shapes everything else. Those who do not fear God end up fearing everything else: people, the future, failure, death. Those who fear God find that this one fear frees them from all the others.

Six units: (1) What the Fear of the Lord Is; (2) Why We Fear Him: The Holiness of God; (3) Fear and Love Together; (4) The Fear of God and the Fear of Man; (5) Lives Shaped by the Fear of the Lord; (6) The Fruit and Blessing of Fearing God. This study is a companion to the study on Biblical Wisdom, which shows how the fear of the Lord is the beginning of a wise life.

1.title: What the Fear of the Lord Is
1.overview:
At Mount Sinai the people of Israel saw thunder, lightning and smoke, and heard the sound of the trumpet. They were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off (Exod 20:18). They begged Moses to speak to them instead of God. Then Moses said something that sounds at first like a contradiction: Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin (Exod 20:20).

Do not fear, so that you may fear. Moses was distinguishing two kinds of fear. One is the fear that runs away from God, terrified and hiding. The other is the fear that stays near to God, humbled and reverent, and keeps a person from sin. The first kind keeps its distance. The second draws near on God's terms. God did not want his people to flee from him in panic. He wanted them to know him so truly that they would never take him lightly.

The fear of the Lord, then, is not mainly an emotion, though it can include strong feelings. It is a settled orientation of the heart toward God. It means taking God seriously: his greatness, his holiness, his word, his authority and his judgment. It means living every part of life before his face, knowing that The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good (Prov 15:3). And it always leads to obedience. Again and again Scripture joins fearing God with walking in his ways. Moses summed up God's whole requirement this way: to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul (Deut 10:12).

Notice that love is in that list too. Fear and love are not opposites in Scripture. They grow from the same root, which is a true knowledge of who God is.
1.theology:
Two kinds of fear: Christians have long distinguished between the fear of a slave and the fear of a son. A slave fears punishment and wishes he could escape his master. A son reveres his father, fears displeasing him, and would not want to be anywhere else. The first is the fear of the unbeliever before the Judge. The second is the fear of the believer before the Father.

A whole-life response: In Scripture the fear of the LORD is so central that it can stand for true religion as a whole. When Proverbs says The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge (Prov 1:7), it means that a right relationship to God is the foundation of everything else.

Its absence is the root of sin: When Paul sums up the condition of fallen humanity in Romans 3, he ends with this line: There is no fear of God before their eyes (Rom 3:18). Every other sin in his list flows from that one. People who do not fear God will eventually do anything.

A gift of grace: God promises in the new covenant, I will put the fear of me in their hearts, that they may not turn from me (Jer 32:40). The right fear of God is not something we manufacture. It is something God plants in the hearts of his people, and it keeps them from falling away.
1.examples:
Then: When Jesus calmed the storm on the Sea of Galilee, the disciples had been terrified of the wind and the waves. But when the storm stopped, Mark says they were filled with great fear and said to one another, "Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?" (Mark 4:41). Their fear did not disappear when the danger passed. It increased, and it changed direction. They had been afraid of the storm. Now they were in awe of the one who commands storms.

Now: A man is alone in a hotel room on a business trip, with a laptop and no one to see what he watches. What keeps him pure? Not the fear of being caught, since no one will know. Only the knowledge that God sees, and that he would grieve the Father who loves him. That is the fear of the Lord at work. Like Joseph, he asks, How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God? (Gen 39:9).

A simple test: Ask yourself whom you think of when you are tempted to do wrong in secret. If the only question is "Will anyone find out?" the fear of God is weak in you. If the question is "What will this mean before God?" it is growing.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die." Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The people's fear at Sinai was real, and in one sense it was right. God is terrifying in his holiness. But their response was to stand far off and ask that God not speak to them. Moses answered with a different fear, one that would keep them from sin rather than from God. This passage teaches us that the purpose of God's majesty is not to drive us away but to make us take him seriously. The fear God wants produces holiness, not hiding.

verseByVerse.quote: "And now, Israel, what does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, to serve the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses gathers up everything God asks of his people in one sentence, and it begins with fear. Then it moves at once to walking in his ways, loving him and serving him with the whole heart. These are not five separate duties but five sides of one life lived toward God. To fear God is to love him with reverence. To love God is to fear him with delight. A person who claims to love God but does not fear him, or to fear God but does not love him, has not yet understood who God is.

verseByVerse.quote: The eyes of the LORD are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The fear of the Lord begins with the simple awareness that God sees. His eyes are in every place. They see the good done in secret and the evil done in secret. For the wicked this is a terrifying truth. For the believer it is both a warning and a comfort. It warns us that no sin is hidden. It comforts us that no faithfulness is overlooked, no tear unseen, no prayer unheard. Living before God's eyes is the root of integrity.

verseByVerse.quote: "There is no fear of God before their eyes." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul quotes Psalm 36 to sum up the human condition apart from grace. After a long list of sins of the tongue, the hands and the feet, he names the root: There is no fear of God before their eyes. People sin freely because they do not take God seriously. They live as though he were absent, or harmless, or would never judge. The beginning of salvation is often the moment when a person first truly fears God, and then discovers the mercy that the fearful need.

1.reflection:
Before this study, what did you think "the fear of the Lord" meant? Where did that idea come from?

Read Exodus 20:18-21. What is the difference between the fear that keeps people far off and the fear Moses wanted them to have?

In what situations are you most aware that God sees you? In what situations do you tend to forget?

Why do you think Paul names the lack of the fear of God as the root of all the sins in Romans 3?

2.title: Why We Fear Him: The Holiness of God
2.overview:
We fear God because of who he is. In the year King Uzziah died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up (Isa 6:1). Seraphim, creatures who had never sinned, covered their faces and their feet before him and called to one another, Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory! (Isa 6:3). The doorposts shook. Smoke filled the house.

And Isaiah, the most righteous man in Jerusalem, cried out, Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips (Isa 6:5). Before he saw God, he could pronounce woes on others. When he saw God, he pronounced a woe on himself. That is what happens when a sinner sees the holiness of God. Every excuse disappears.

God's holiness means that he is utterly set apart: above and beyond everything he has made, and perfectly pure, without the smallest trace of evil. He is the Creator and we are creatures. He is the Judge and we will give account. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb 10:31). This is not an Old Testament idea left behind. Hebrews, writing to Christians, says that because we have received an unshakable kingdom we must worship with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire (Heb 12:28-29).

Our age has largely lost this sense of God's weight and majesty. God is often spoken of as a friendly helper or a therapist. He is kind beyond words, but he is never small. And it is only when we see how holy he is that we begin to understand how amazing his grace is. Isaiah's woe was followed at once by a burning coal from the altar and the words, your guilt is taken away, and your sin atoned for (Isa 6:7).
2.theology:
The fear of the Creator: Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the inhabitants of the world stand in awe of him! (Ps 33:8). The psalm grounds this in creation: he spoke and it came to be. Every human being owes God reverence simply because he made us.

The fear of the Judge: Jesus said, Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell (Matt 10:28). The same Jesus who welcomed sinners warned plainly of judgment. Paul writes that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, and then, Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others (2 Cor 5:10-11). The coming judgment is one of the reasons Christians take evangelism seriously.

The fear of the Redeemer: Strikingly, Scripture also says we fear God because of his grace. Peter tells believers to live in fear, knowing that you were ransomed ... with the precious blood of Christ (1 Pet 1:18-19). The price of our redemption shows how seriously God takes sin and how much he has given. Those who understand the cross will never treat God lightly.

Reverence in worship: I will bow down toward your holy temple in the fear of you (Ps 5:7). Worship should be joyful, but never casual. The God we approach as Father is the same God before whom angels cover their faces.
2.examples:
Then: When Peter saw the miraculous catch of fish, he did not shout for joy. He fell down at Jesus' knees, saying, "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." (Luke 5:8). Like Isaiah, he saw holiness, and saw himself. And like Isaiah, he was not sent away but called: from now on he would catch men.

Then: In the early church, Ananias and Sapphira lied to the Holy Spirit and fell dead. Luke records, And great fear came upon the whole church and upon all who heard of these things (Acts 5:11). God was teaching the new covenant community that grace does not make him less holy.

Now: A church service is full of energy and noise, but almost nothing in it suggests that the people are standing before a holy God. Another church is reverent but cold. Neither is what Scripture describes. The psalmist joined both: Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling (Ps 2:11). Joyful reverence and reverent joy belong together, in a congregation and in a single heart.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and the train of his robe filled the temple. Above him stood the seraphim. Each had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew. And one called to another and said: "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke. And I said: "Woe is me! For I am lost; for I am a man of unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people of unclean lips; for my eyes have seen the King, the LORD of hosts!" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The vision begins with a date: In the year that King Uzziah died. A long and prosperous reign had ended, and the nation's future was uncertain. Isaiah went into the temple and saw the true King, still on his throne. The seraphim cry Holy three times; repetition is how Hebrew gives emphasis, and a threefold repetition is rare. And Isaiah's response is not curiosity but undoing. Real encounters with God's holiness always humble. Anyone who claims to have seen God and comes away proud has not seen him.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The writer has just contrasted Mount Sinai, with its fire and darkness, with Mount Zion, the city of the living God, where Christians have come by grace. You might expect him to say that the fear of Sinai is now gone. Instead he says that because our privilege is greater, our reverence must be deeper. Our God is a consuming fire. He has not changed. Grace does not make God tame. It makes it possible for sinners to approach the fire and not be destroyed.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell. Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? And not one of them will fall to the ground apart from your Father. But even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In the space of four verses Jesus tells his disciples to fear and not to fear. Fear him who can destroy soul and body in hell. Then, about that same God: not a sparrow falls without your Father, the hairs of your head are numbered, Fear not, therefore. The God who is to be feared above all is the same God who cares for his children in every detail. Those who fear him need fear nothing else. This is the logic of the whole study in a single passage.

verseByVerse.quote: For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive what is due for what he has done in the body, whether good or evil. Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. But what we are is known to God, and I hope it is known also to your conscience. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul, the apostle of grace, lived in the awareness that he would stand before Christ's judgment seat. For believers this is not a judgment that decides salvation, which is secure in Christ. It is the assessment of how we have lived as his servants. That knowledge made Paul earnest. Knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade others. The fear of the Lord does not make Christians timid. It makes them urgent, faithful and bold.

2.reflection:
Read Isaiah 6:1-8. What moved Isaiah from "Woe is me" to "Here I am! Send me"?

In what ways does our culture, and sometimes the church, make God seem small?

How does the cross deepen, rather than remove, the believer's reverence for God?

Does your worship, private and public, reflect both joy and reverence? What would help?

3.title: Fear and Love Together
3.overview:
Many Christians feel a tension here. John writes, There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment (1 John 4:18). Paul says, you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons (Rom 8:15). Yet the same New Testament tells believers to fear God. How do these fit together?

The answer is in John's own explanation: the fear that love casts out is the fear that has to do with punishment. A believer in Christ need not fear God's condemnation, because Christ has borne it. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1). The terror of the guilty before the Judge is gone. What remains, and grows, is the reverent awe of a child before a holy Father.

In fact, Scripture says that grace produces the right kind of fear. But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared (Ps 130:4). That is surprising. We might expect forgiveness to make people careless. But true forgiveness, understood rightly, makes a person tremble with grateful wonder. The more we understand what it cost God to forgive us, the less lightly we will treat him.

The Psalms join fear and love constantly. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him (Ps 103:13). The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him (Ps 25:14). The LORD takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love (Ps 147:11). The people who fear God are the people God draws close to. The fear of the Lord is not distance from God. It is the reverent intimacy of those who know him best.
3.theology:
Filial, not servile: The believer's fear is the fear of a son, not of a slave. It is shaped by adoption. We cry Abba! Father!, and we also remember that our Father judges impartially according to each one's deeds (1 Pet 1:17). Both truths keep us humble and secure.

Fear grows with love: In human relationships, the more we love someone, the more we fear to hurt them. A child who loves a good father fears grieving him more than fearing punishment. So with God. Mature Christians do not fear God less than new believers. They fear him more, and love him more, at the same time.

Mercy for those who fear: Mary sang, And his mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation (Luke 1:50). God's steadfast love is repeatedly promised to those who fear him (Ps 103:11, 17). Fear of the Lord is not a barrier to grace. It is the posture in which grace is received.

Assurance and reverence: Some fear that taking God's holiness seriously will rob them of assurance. The opposite is true. Assurance rests on Christ's finished work, not on our feelings. And it is those who are secure in his love who can most freely stand in awe of his holiness without being crushed by it.
3.examples:
Then: Abraham obeyed God when asked to offer Isaac, and the angel said, for now I know that you fear God, seeing you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me (Gen 22:12). Abraham's fear was not terror. It was a love for God greater than his love for the son he had waited for, and a trust that God would provide.

Now: A young Christian who grew up in a harsh, fearful home finds the idea of fearing God frightening. She hears it as being afraid of a father who might explode. She needs to hear both halves of the truth. The punishing fear is gone for those in Christ; God is not an angry father waiting to strike. And the God who loves her is so holy, so great and so good that the right response is awe, worship and a desire never to grieve him.

Now: An older believer, after decades of walking with God, says that the more she knows him, the more she trembles at his greatness and the more she rests in his love. That is not contradiction. It is maturity.

verseByVerse.quote: If you, O LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But with you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The psalmist faces the worst question a person can ask: if God kept a record of every sin, who could stand? The answer is no one. Then comes the great But: with you there is forgiveness. And the purpose of forgiveness is that you may be feared. Forgiveness does not make God cheap. It shows us a God who is holy enough to see every sin and merciful enough to remove it. That combination produces awe. People who think God overlooks sin easily do not fear him. People who know what forgiveness cost do.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear. For fear has to do with punishment, and whoever fears has not been perfected in love. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: John is writing about assurance on the day of judgment (1 John 4:17). The fear he means is the fear of punishment, the dread of a guilty person facing condemnation. Perfect love, God's love for us in Christ received and growing in us, drives that fear out. This verse does not mean that believers should have no reverence for God. It means that those who are loved by God need not dread his judgment. The terror is gone; the awe remains.

verseByVerse.quote: For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, "Abba! Father!" (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul contrasts two spirits: the spirit of slavery, which leads back into fear, and the Spirit of adoption, who teaches us to cry Abba! Father! The Christian life is not lived in the anxious fear of a slave who never knows if he has done enough. It is lived as sons and daughters who are secure in the Father's house. Yet a good father is still honoured. Adoption does not remove reverence. It transforms it from dread into love.

verseByVerse.quote: For as high as the heavens are above the earth, so great is his steadfast love toward those who fear him; as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions from us. As a father shows compassion to his children, so the LORD shows compassion to those who fear him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Three times in this psalm God's love is promised to those who fear him (vv.11, 13, 17). His steadfast love is as high as the heavens. He removes our sins as far as the east is from the west. He shows compassion like a father. The fear of the Lord is the doorway to this love, not a barrier against it. Those who come to God in humble reverence find him to be the most tender of fathers.

3.reflection:
How would you explain to a friend the difference between the fear 1 John 4:18 says love casts out and the fear believers are called to have?

Read Psalm 130. Why does forgiveness lead to fearing God rather than taking him lightly?

Does your experience of God lean more toward fear without love, or love without reverence? What truth do you most need to hear?

How does knowing God as Father shape the way you fear him?

4.title: The Fear of God and the Fear of Man
4.overview:
Everyone fears something. The question is not whether we will fear but what we will fear. And Scripture teaches that the fear of God and the fear of man are rivals. Whichever is stronger will rule us.

The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe (Prov 29:25). The fear of man is a trap. It shows itself in people-pleasing, a craving for approval, dread of criticism, compromise to avoid conflict, silence when we should speak, and lies to protect our image. It can rule a teenager desperate to fit in, a pastor afraid of his congregation, an employee afraid of losing a job, or a parent afraid of a child's displeasure.

God's answer is not to tell us to stop fearing altogether, but to fear the right one. Isaiah was told, do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread (Isa 8:12-13). When God is big in our eyes, people shrink to their proper size. They are still to be loved and served, but they are no longer our masters.

Jesus said the same: do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear (Luke 12:4-5). The worst that people can do to us is limited. God's authority is not. And this same God numbers the hairs of our heads. The person who fears God need not be ruled by anyone else.

Paul felt the pull of the fear of man and refused it: For am I now seeking the approval of man, or of God? ... If I were still trying to please man, I would not be a servant of Christ (Gal 1:10). Every Christian faces that choice, often many times a day.
4.theology:
What we fear, we serve: Fear is a form of worship. Whatever we fear most, we will obey. If we fear people most, we will do what pleases them. If we fear God most, we will do what pleases him, even when people object.

The cure is a bigger God: The fear of man is not cured mainly by self-esteem or confidence. It is cured by seeing God as he is. When God is great in our eyes, the opinions of others matter less. When we know we are fully accepted in Christ, we no longer need the approval of others to feel secure.

Love without fear of man: Freedom from the fear of man does not make Christians careless about people. It frees us to love them truly: to tell them hard truths, to serve them without needing their thanks, and to forgive them when they reject us. People-pleasers cannot really love, because they are always protecting themselves.

Courage is the fruit: He is not afraid of bad news; his heart is firm, trusting in the LORD (Ps 112:7). The man who fears the LORD in verse 1 of that psalm is the man who is not afraid in verse 7. The fear of God is the source of Christian courage.
4.examples:
Then: Pharaoh ordered the Hebrew midwives to kill every newborn boy. But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live (Exod 1:17). Two ordinary women defied the most powerful man in the world because they feared someone greater. And God blessed them: And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families (Exod 1:21).

Then: When Nehemiah became governor, the officials before him had taxed the people heavily and let their servants lord it over them. Nehemiah refused: But I did not do so, because of the fear of God (Neh 5:15). The fear of God governed how he used power and money.

Now: A teenager's friends are mocking another student online. Joining in would make him popular; refusing will make him a target. Fearing God, he refuses, and quietly messages the victim with kindness.

Now: A pastor knows a passage of Scripture will offend some influential members. The fear of man says, "Skip it." The fear of God says, "Preach it faithfully, with love." He preaches it, and trusts God with the consequences.

Now: An employee is pressured by a manager to falsify figures. Fearing God more than her boss, she refuses respectfully, and is ready to accept the cost.

verseByVerse.quote: The fear of man lays a snare, but whoever trusts in the LORD is safe. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: A snare is a hidden trap that catches an animal by the foot and holds it fast. The fear of man works like that. It rarely looks dangerous. It looks like being nice, keeping the peace or being sensible. But it catches us and holds us, until we cannot do what is right because we are afraid of what others will think. The alternative is not self-confidence but trust: whoever trusts in the LORD is safe. Safety does not come from keeping everyone happy. It comes from resting in God.

verseByVerse.quote: "Do not call conspiracy all that this people calls conspiracy, and do not fear what they fear, nor be in dread. But the LORD of hosts, him you shall honor as holy. Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Judah was in a panic over a military alliance against it. Everyone was talking about conspiracy and danger. God told Isaiah not to join the national mood: do not fear what they fear. Instead, Let him be your fear, and let him be your dread. In every generation the crowd has its fears, whether political, economic or cultural, and Christians are tempted to share them. This verse calls us to a different centre. Peter later applies this passage to Christians facing persecution (1 Pet 3:14-15).

verseByVerse.quote: "I tell you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body, and after that have nothing more that they can do. But I will warn you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has authority to cast into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jesus calls his disciples my friends and then gives them a warning. He is not threatening them; he is protecting them. People can kill the body, but that is all they can do. God has authority over eternity. Jesus repeats it for emphasis: Yes, I tell you, fear him! And in the next breath he speaks of sparrows and the hairs of your head (Luke 12:6-7). The God to be feared is the Father who cares. Fearing him rightly sets us free from every lesser fear.

verseByVerse.quote: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the first acts of civil disobedience recorded in Scripture, and it is done by two women whose names are recorded, Shiphrah and Puah (Exod 1:15), while the Pharaoh's name is not given. Their obedience was costly and dangerous. They had no army, no position and no guarantee of protection. They simply feared God more than the king. Their story shows that the fear of the Lord is not only a private feeling. It shapes courageous action in the public world.

4.reflection:
Where do you see the fear of man most in your own life: approval, criticism, conflict, reputation?

Read Isaiah 8:11-14. What fears does the crowd around you share, and how should fearing God reshape them?

Think of a time when the fear of man caused you to stay silent or compromise. What would the fear of God have led you to do?

How does knowing you are fully accepted in Christ free you from the need for others' approval?

5.title: Lives Shaped by the Fear of the Lord
5.overview:
Scripture does not only teach the fear of the Lord. It shows what it looks like in real lives. Again and again the Bible describes its heroes simply as people who feared God.

Job is introduced as a man who was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil (Job 1:1). God himself repeats the description (Job 1:8). His fear of God was tested by unimaginable loss, and it held.

Joseph refused the advances of Potiphar's wife because sin would be against God (Gen 39:9). Years later, as ruler of Egypt, he reassured his frightened brothers with the words, for I fear God (Gen 42:18). His fear of God made him trustworthy in power.

Obadiah, a servant in wicked King Ahab's palace, feared the LORD greatly (1 Kgs 18:3). When Queen Jezebel was killing the prophets, he hid a hundred of them in caves and fed them. He had feared the LORD from my youth (1 Kgs 18:12). A believer in a hostile workplace, he used his position to protect God's people.

Cornelius, a Roman centurion, was a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God (Acts 10:2). God sent Peter to him with the gospel, and he became one of the first Gentile converts.

And Jonah, even while running from God, could say, I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land (Jonah 1:9). The irony is sharp. The pagan sailors, seeing God's power in the storm, feared the LORD exceedingly (Jonah 1:16), while the prophet who confessed the fear of the Lord was fleeing from him. Confessing the fear of the Lord with our lips is not the same as living it.
5.theology:
Christ, the one who perfectly feared God: Isaiah foretold that the Spirit would rest on the Messiah as the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD (Isa 11:2), and that his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD (Isa 11:3). Jesus did not merely tolerate this fear; he delighted in it. In Gethsemane he prayed with loud cries and tears, and he was heard because of his reverence (Heb 5:7). He is the true God-fearing man, and his perfect reverence is counted to those who trust in him.

The church in the fear of the Lord: The early church was marked by both fear and comfort: walking in the fear of the Lord and in the comfort of the Holy Spirit, it multiplied (Acts 9:31). Reverence and joy, holiness and growth went together.

Sanctification in fear: let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of body and spirit, bringing holiness to completion in the fear of God (2 Cor 7:1). Growing in holiness is not driven by guilt or pride, but by reverence for the God who has made us his own.

Working out salvation: Paul tells believers to work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for it is God who works in you (Phil 2:12-13). The trembling is not fear of losing salvation, but awe at the fact that the almighty God is at work within us.
5.examples:
Obadiah today: A Christian civil servant works in a department whose policies often oppose Christian convictions. She does not quit in protest or blend in. She does excellent work, quietly protects colleagues who are treated unfairly, and refuses to take part in anything dishonest. Like Obadiah, she fears the LORD greatly in a hostile place.

Cornelius today: A businessman who is not yet a Christian is generous, prays and leads his family in respect for God. A Christian colleague, seeing his openness, invites him to read the Gospel of John together. Cornelius reminds us that God often prepares hearts before he sends the messenger.

Jonah today: A church member speaks fluently about reverence for God, but harbours bitterness and refuses God's call to forgive someone who wronged him. His words and his life do not match. The fear of the Lord is proved by obedience, not by vocabulary.

verseByVerse.quote: There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job, and that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The book of Job introduces its hero with four phrases: blameless, upright, one who feared God and one who turned away from evil. The fear of God sits at the centre of his character and shows itself in turning from evil. The rest of the book tests whether Job feared God only because God blessed him (Job 1:9). Through grief, sickness and confusion, Job's fear of God survived, even when he did not understand God's ways. True fear of God is not a reward for blessing. It continues when blessing is taken away.

verseByVerse.quote: And Ahab called Obadiah, who was over the household. (Now Obadiah feared the LORD greatly, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Ahab and Jezebel were among the most wicked rulers in Israel's history, and Obadiah managed their household. Yet the text says plainly that he feared the LORD greatly. He did not need to leave his job to be faithful. He used his position to save a hundred prophets. Some believers are called to leave corrupt situations; others, like Obadiah, are placed there by God to protect his people. The fear of the Lord gives wisdom to know which, and courage to act.

verseByVerse.quote: a devout man who feared God with all his household, gave alms generously to the people, and prayed continually to God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Cornelius was a soldier of the occupying Roman army, a Gentile, and an outsider to Israel. Yet Luke describes him as one who feared God with all his household. His reverence showed itself in generosity and prayer. And God answered him by sending the gospel. Fearing God was not the end of Cornelius's story. It was the beginning, leading him to faith in Christ. The fear of the Lord always points beyond itself to the Savior.

verseByVerse.quote: In the days of his flesh, Jesus offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, to him who was able to save him from death, and he was heard because of his reverence. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This verse lets us see into Gethsemane. Jesus prayed with loud cries and tears, and he was heard because of his reverence. The Son of God, facing the cross, prayed in godly fear. He did not demand. He submitted: not my will but yours. His reverence was perfect, and so his prayer was heard, not by escaping death but by being raised from it. Our fear of God is weak and mixed. His was complete, and we are accepted in him.

5.reflection:
Which of the people in this unit, Job, Joseph, Obadiah, Cornelius, best shows what the fear of the Lord looks like for you right now?

Obadiah feared the LORD in a hostile workplace. Where are you called to fear God in a place that does not?

Jonah confessed the fear of the LORD while running from him. Where might your words about God be ahead of your obedience?

How does Jesus' perfect reverence (Heb 5:7) encourage you when your own fear of God is weak?

6.title: The Fruit and Blessing of Fearing God
6.overview:
The fear of the Lord is not a gloomy burden. Scripture repeatedly describes it as the path to life, joy and security. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death (Prov 14:27). The fear of the LORD leads to life, and whoever has it rests satisfied (Prov 19:23).

Those who fear God are promised his friendship (Ps 25:14), his compassion (Ps 103:13), his provision: Oh, fear the LORD, you his saints, for those who fear him have no lack! (Ps 34:9), and his storehouse of goodness: Oh, how abundant is your goodness, which you have stored up for those who fear you (Ps 31:19). They have a refuge for themselves and their children: In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge (Prov 14:26).

The fear of the Lord also shapes character. The fear of the LORD is hatred of evil (Prov 8:13). It makes us humble, honest and pure. It frees us from envy: Let not your heart envy sinners, but continue in the fear of the LORD all the day (Prov 23:17). And it makes ordinary life rich: Better is a little with the fear of the LORD than great treasure and trouble with it (Prov 15:16).

How does this fear grow? By looking at God. We grow in the fear of the Lord as we read his word, which reveals his holiness and grace; as we worship with his people; as we pray with reverence; as we remember the cross; and as we keep the coming judgment and the coming glory before our eyes. The psalmist prayed, unite my heart to fear your name (Ps 86:11). We can pray the same, and God has promised to answer.

And one day all creation will join in. The redeemed in heaven sing, Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy (Rev 15:4). The fear of the Lord is not only for this life. It is the eternal posture of the redeemed, full of joy, before the throne.
6.theology:
Blessing, not merit: The blessings promised to those who fear God are not wages earned. They are the fruit of a right relationship with God, which is itself his gift. God gives the fear, and then delights in those who have it.

Proverbs, not guarantees: As the Biblical Wisdom study explains, promises in Proverbs describe how God's world normally works. God-fearing people still suffer, as Job did. But in every circumstance they have the deeper blessings: God's presence, his friendship and an eternal inheritance.

Remembered by God: In Malachi's day, when many had grown cynical, those who feared the LORD spoke with one another. The LORD paid attention and heard them, and a book of remembrance was written before him (Mal 3:16). God notices those who fear him, even when the world does not.

The whole duty: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man (Eccl 12:13). After all the searching of Ecclesiastes, this is the conclusion. The fear of God is not one virtue among many. It is the shape of a life lived rightly before him.
6.examples:
Then: After the crossing of the Red Sea, the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in his servant Moses (Exod 14:31). Fear and faith grew together as they saw what God had done. Then they sang (Exod 15).

Now: A couple facing financial hardship decide to keep giving to their church and to the poor, trusting God's care. They do not become wealthy. But they find that a little with the fear of the LORD is richer than they imagined: contentment, peace in their home, and children who learn that God can be trusted.

Now: A small group decides to meet each week to read Scripture and encourage one another, as those in Malachi's day did. The world takes no notice. But God does, and writes their names in his book of remembrance.

Growing the fear of God this week: Read Isaiah 6 or Revelation 4 slowly. Begin prayer by adoring God before asking for anything. Before a decision, ask, "What would honor God as holy here?" At the end of the day, remember one way God showed his greatness and one way he showed his mercy.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fear of the LORD one has strong confidence, and his children will have a refuge. The fear of the LORD is a fountain of life, that one may turn away from the snares of death. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Two pictures sit side by side. The fear of the Lord is a fortress, strong confidence and a refuge for children. And it is a fountain, a source of life that turns us from the snares of death. Fear and confidence are not opposites here. The person who fears God is the most secure person in the world, because the one they fear is also their refuge. And the blessing passes down: his children will have a refuge. A home shaped by the fear of God is a safe place to grow up.

verseByVerse.quote: The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most beautiful promises in the Psalms. The friendship of the LORD is for those who fear him. It is close, confidential fellowship, the kind of conversation reserved for trusted friends. The holy God, before whom angels cover their faces, draws near in friendship to those who fear him. Reverence does not keep God at a distance. It is the way into his closest fellowship.

verseByVerse.quote: Teach me your way, O LORD, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: David asks for two things: to be taught God's way, and for God to unite my heart to fear your name. Our hearts are divided. Part of us fears God, and part of us fears people, failure, loss or the future. David asks God to gather all those scattered loyalties into one undivided reverence. It is a prayer every Christian can pray daily, and it is a prayer God loves to answer, because he promised in the new covenant to put his fear in our hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? For you alone are holy. All nations will come and worship you, for your righteous acts have been revealed." (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: This is the song of those who have conquered by the blood of the Lamb. And their question is rhetorical: Who will not fear, O Lord, and glorify your name? In the end, everyone will see God as he is. The fear of the Lord will no longer be rare. All nations will come and worship you. For the redeemed, that fear will be pure joy, the awe of beholding the holy God forever. To fear him now is to begin to live the life of heaven on earth.

6.reflection:
Which promise to those who fear God in this unit means the most to you, and why?

Read Malachi 3:16-18. How does it encourage you that God notices those who fear him, even when the world does not?

Pray Psalm 86:11 for yourself. Where is your heart divided between fearing God and fearing something else?

Choose one habit from this unit to help you grow in the fear of the Lord this week.
